Title: Arbitrary Code Execution via Python eval() in ORM Class Registry and Type De-stringification
Analysis:
In SQLAlchemy, when defining relationships or parsing string annotations in a Declarative model, Python's built-in `eval()` function is used to resolve classes/types from string arguments. 

In `lib/sqlalchemy/orm/clsregistry.py`, specifically inside `_class_resolver.__call__`, string expressions are parsed using `eval(self.arg, globals(), self._dict)`. 
Furthermore, in `lib/sqlalchemy/util/typing.py`, `eval_expression()` uses `eval(expression, cls_namespace, locals_)` to de-stringify Python type annotations (e.g. `Mapped['MyClass']`).

Although this is standard dual-use/metaprogramming behavior in Python ORM frameworks to dynamically resolve relationships and annotations during import/mapper initialization time, it can act as a code execution vector if untrusted user input is passed into a dynamic model or database schema generation mechanism (for instance, dynamically generating relationships or tables from user-controlled JSON schemas or YAML models).

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
To trigger arbitrary code execution, a developer would have to pass a malicious string to a relationship or annotation:
`relationship("__import__('os').system('id')")` or `Mapped["__import__('os').system('id')"]`

While this is intended behavior within SQLAlchemy's architecture (to support complex python-like expressions in relationships), it represents a critical code execution sink when the model definitions themselves are loaded from untrusted metadata/configurations.

Title: Arbitrary Code Execution via Python eval() in Type Annotation De-stringifier
Analysis:
In SQLAlchemy, de-stringifying annotations (e.g. from `from __future__ import annotations`) relies on the utility function `eval_expression` in `lib/sqlalchemy/util/typing.py`. 
Inside `eval_expression()`, `eval(expression, cls_namespace, locals_)` (or `eval(expression, base_globals, locals_)`) is invoked to evaluate Python type annotations specified as strings.

If a schema definition or class definition is constructed dynamically from user-controlled specifications (e.g., dynamically compiling Python code or creating a dynamic class with typing annotations specified from JSON or YAML data), this leads to arbitrary code execution.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
`de_stringify_annotation(MyClass, "__import__('os').system('id')", "my_module", {})`

While it is standard dual-use/metaprogramming behavior in Python ORM frameworks to dynamically resolve relationships and annotations, it represents a code execution sink when the model annotations are populated from untrusted input.
